results.title: Model Artifacts | AI Glossary by Posium
results.content: # Model Artifacts Model artifacts are the tangible outputs produced during the lifecycle of a machine learning model, including the trained model, metadata, and associated files necessary for deployment and reproducibility. **What Constitutes a Model Artifact?** * **The Trained Model:** This is the core artifact, representing the learned parameters and structure of the machine learning model. **Importance of Model Artifacts** * **Reproducibility:** Artifacts enable the reproduction of the model's training process and results. **Model Artifact Management** Effective model artifact management is a key aspect of MLOps (Machine Learning Operations). Tools and platforms are available to help manage the lifecycle of model artifacts, including versioning, storage, and deployment. In summary, model artifacts are more than just the trained model file.

results.title: How OCI Artifacts will drive future AI use cases | CNCF
results.content: # How OCI Artifacts will drive future AI use cases. ## The role of OCI artifacts in the AI ecosystem. The CNCF ModelPack Specification builds on top of OCI artifacts and aims to standardize the packaging, distribution, and execution of AI models in cloud native environments. * **Standardized AI/ML model packaging**: With OCI artifacts, models can be versioned, distributed, and tracked like container images. * **AI/ML model development**: For example, it is possible to package ML pipelines as OCI artifacts reuse and sharing across teams. Having standards around OCI artifacts are essential for building robust AI features into Kubernetes. Image volumes could also support OCI artifacts as a special use case. ## CRI-O and OCI Artifact support. Recent versions of CRI-O have added native support for OCI artifacts, storing them in a dedicated directory to keep them separate from traditional container image layouts. * Mounting OCI artifacts as image volumes in Kubernetes.

results.title: Beyond the Basics: What Truly Open Source AI Could Include
results.content: ### The Standard Ingredients of Open Source AI Before diving into what more is required, its worth recapping the widely accepted baseline for open-source AI: * Code and Model Artifacts: The complete source code, model weights, and training code. Full Training Pipelines and Environment Details: A truly open source AI project should share not only the training code but also exhaustive details about the training pipeline. ### Comprehensive Documentation and Model Cards While code comments and basic documentation are useful, open-source AI should provide an array of supporting documents that explain every facet of the system. a. Open Licenses for Every Component: While many projects release their code under MIT, Apache, or GPL licenses, a genuinely open source AI must apply similarly permissive licenses to all its componentsincluding training data (when legally possible), training scripts, evaluation tools, and even the documentation. ### Detailed Economic and Resource Transparency An often overlooked aspect of open source in AI is the transparency about the economic and resource costs of training and running models. For DeepSeek (or any future AI system) to be truly open source, it should adopt the comprehensive practices weve outlined: * Provide detailed reproducibility artifacts (e.g., intermediate checkpoints, complete logs, full hyperparameter settings). * Revised Open Source AI Definitions: These would require that not only the final model and its weights be available, but that all associated training data (or detailed metadata about it), training pipelines, and evaluation processes are fully documented and shared. * Ethical Licensing: New license types that specifically address AI and its unique challenges could help standardize what is required for a model to be considered truly open source. While releasing code, models, weights, datasets, and diagrams is a critical first step, it is only part of what makes an AI system genuinely open source. For an AI project to be fully open, it must provide: * Detailed reproducibility artifacts that include complete training pipelines, hyperparameter logs, and intermediate checkpoints. As projects like EleutherAIs GPT-Neo and DeepSeeks open-weight models show, the future of AI could be shaped not by a handful of proprietary giants but by a global, transparent, and collaborative network of researchers, developers, and enthusiasts.

results.title: Day 56/100: Experiment Tracking and Model Lineage — Don’t Lose Your Best Work | by Sebastian Buzdugan | Medium
results.content: # Day 56/100: Experiment Tracking and Model Lineage — Don’t Lose Your Best Work. Yesterday, we explored* ***Feature Engineering at Scale****, turning raw data into robust model inputs. Today, we address a silent killer of reproducibility and team collaboration: failing to track your experiments and model versions. Let’s talk about* ***Experiment Tracking*** *and* ***Model Lineage*** *— and how to make your ML workflow both traceable and trusted.*. ## 🎯 Why Experiment Tracking Matters. * “Which hyperparameters did I use for that great model?”. * “What data was that model trained on?”. Then you already know the pain of poor tracking. **Tracking experiments is how you turn hacking into engineering.**. ## 🔎 What Is Experiment Tracking? Experiment tracking involves recording the details of each training run, including:. * Artifacts (model files, logs, visualizations). It builds a **history of your model development**, so you know what changed, when, and why. ## 🧠 What Is Model Lineage? Model lineage takes tracking one step further. * Which **training script** produced the model. It’s the **audit trail** of your model’s life — from experiment to production. ## ⚙️ What You Should Track in Every ML Run. * Output artifacts (model weights, logs, plots). This allows you to **compare apples to apples** when evaluating models. ## 🛠 Tools for Experiment Tracking. * **MLflow** — Open source experiment tracker with UI and model registry. * **Comet.ml** — Team-friendly experiment tracking. * **Neptune.ai** — Flexible tracker with metadata-rich logging. * **Sacred + Omniboard** — Python-based local tracking. * **TensorBoard** — Native to TensorFlow for visual logs. * Link model files to their experiments. ## 🔧 Best Practices for Tracking. * **Log early and often** — even for baseline experiments. * Integrate with **Git** for code version tracking. * Store model artifacts in **cloud buckets** or **registries**. * Automate tracking in your training scripts (use decorators or callbacks). ## 🌱 Model Lineage in Production. Tracking doesn’t end at training. * Which version of the model is deployed. * What data it was retrained on. Tomorrow, we’ll look at **Model Registries and Version Control** — where you store, organize, and serve your models just like software artifacts.
